[2] Colin Lamb's Narrative
[3] 1
[4] According to police records: At 2:59 PM on September 9th, I was walking west on Wilbraham Crescent. This was my first time here, and I must admit, everything about the place left me bewildered.
[5] For some time now, I've had a feeling, and this feeling has been growing stronger and stronger, almost impossible to shake off. That's just how I felt.
[6] I was looking for a house numbered 61, and I thought, maybe I won't find it. I had carefully found houses from 1 to 35, and just then, I discovered that Wilbraham Crescent had reached its end. A road called Albany Avenue rudely blocked my path. I turned around. There were no houses to the north, only a wall. Behind this wall, there were towering modern apartments, and it was clear that the entrance was on another road. It was impossible to find a way from here.
[7] As I walked, I paid attention to the house numbers I passed by – 24, 23, 22, 21, Diana's Cottage (which must be number 20, with an orange cat washing itself on the gatepost), and 19.
[8] The door to number 19 suddenly opened, and a young girl rushed out, then ran up the path. I thought a missile's speed was nothing compared to hers. She ran with such a sharp cry that she looked even more like a missile. The sound was high-pitched and pitiful. The girl ran through the gate and collided with me, almost knocking me off the sidewalk. She not only collided with me but also grabbed me tightly, desperately clinging to me.
[9] "Take it easy," I said, gently shaking her when I regained my balance, "Now take it easy."
[10] The girl's emotions finally calmed down. Although she was still holding on to me tightly, she was no longer screaming, but only panting heavily, gasping and sobbing.
[11] In this situation, I must say that my reaction was not quick enough. I asked her what happened. Realizing that my tone was too weak, I immediately changed it.
[12] "What happened?"
[13] The girl took a deep breath.
[14] "Over there!" She pointed to the place behind her.
[15] "Then what?"
[16] "There was a man lying on the floor... dead... she was about to step on him."
[17] "Who? How did this happen?"
[18] "I think, because she's blind. And there was blood on him."
[19] "Indeed, there was blood." I said, looking at the stain on my sleeve. "Now I'm the same." I pointed to the stain. Thinking about the current situation, I sighed. "You should take me there to see."
[20] But she began to shake her head vigorously.
[21] "I can't go, I can't go... I don't want to go back there."
[22] "Maybe you're right." I looked around. There didn't seem to be a place to put a girl who was about to faint. I gently guided her, letting her lean against the iron railing.
[23] "Stay here," I said, "don't leave until I come back. I won't be long." I leaned forward and if you feel uncomfortable, put your head between your knees, it will feel better."
[24] "I, I think I'm okay now."
[25] Although she said so, she was still a little shaken, but I didn't want to talk to her too much. I gently patted her shoulder, comforted her, and then walked quickly up the path. I went through the door into the house, hesitated slightly in the hallway, observed the left door, which was an empty restaurant, and then walked through the foyer into the opposite living room.
[26] The first thing I saw was an old woman with gray hair sitting on a chair. When I went in, her head turned quickly towards me and said,
[27] "Who came?"
[28] I immediately realized that the woman's eyes were blind. Her eyes looked straight at me, then swept past me and landed on the back of my left ear.
[29] I said directly:
[30] "A young girl ran up the street, saying that someone died here."
[31] I felt that what I said was absurd. In this clean room, the woman sat with her hands folded on the chair, looking so calm. It seemed impossible to find a dead man here.
[32] But she immediately answered.
[33] "Behind the sofa," she said.
[34] I went around the corner of the sofa. Then I saw the open arms, the vacant eyes, and the congealed blood clots.
[35] "How did this happen?" I suddenly asked.
[36] "I don't know."
[37] "So, who is he?"
[38] "I don't know."
[39] "We have to call the police." I look around. "Where's the phone?" "I don't have a phone."
[40] I stare at her intently.
[41] "Are you living here? Is this your house?"
[42] "Yes."
[43] "Can you tell me what happened?"
[44] "Of course. I came back with my shopping -" I noticed the shopping bag thrown on the chair near the door. "I came home and immediately sensed that there was someone else in the house. A blind person is very sensitive to such things. I asked who was in the house. No one answered me. I only heard someone breathing heavily. I went towards the source of the sound. Then someone yelled out - someone had died, I was about to step on the body. Then someone screamed past me, running out of the room."
[45] I nodded. They both told the same story.
[46] "What did you do then?"
[47] "I walked carefully until my foot touched something."
[48] "What happened next?"
[49] "I squatted down. I felt a man's hand. It was cold and there was no pulse… I got up and walked over here, sat down and waited for someone to come. It won't be long, someone will come. That young woman, whoever she is, will call for help. I think it's best not to leave this house."
[50] I was shocked by the woman's calmness. She didn't scream or panic in the house, she just sat there quietly waiting. She was rational, but we still had to take action.
[51] She questioned:
[52] "Who are you?"
[53] "My name is Colin Lamb. I just happened to pass by."
[54] "Where did the young girl go?"
[55] "I let her rest near the entrance. She was scared. Where is the nearest place to call for help?"
[56] "Follow this path for about fifty yards, and there's a phone booth just before the corner."
[57] "Yes, I remember passing by there. I'm going to call the police. You—" I hesitated.
[58] I didn't know whether to say "Are you going to stay here?" or "Are you okay?"
[59] She spared me the decision.
[60] "You should bring the girl inside," she said firmly.
[61] "I don't know if she'll come," I said skeptically.
[62] "Of course, don't let her come into this room. Tell her to wait in the dining room next to the entrance. Tell her I'm brewing tea for her."
[63] She approached me.
[64] "But can you do that?" she asked.
[65] A slight smirk appeared on her face.
[66] "My dear young man, since I moved into this house fourteen years ago, I have been cooking in the kitchen myself. Being blind doesn't mean I'm useless."
[67] "I'm sorry, I was too ignorant. Perhaps I can ask for your name?"
[68] "Millee Pema-Chhoe – Miss."
[69] I left the room and walked out along the path. The girl saw me and struggled to get up.
[70] "I, I think I'm almost better now."
[71] I helped her stand up, smiling,
[72] "That's good."
[73] "There, there, someone died, right?"
[74] I immediately nodded.
[75] "Indeed. I'm going to the phone booth to report the incident to the police. If I were you, I would wait in the house. Go to the restaurant and wait on your left as you enter. Miss Millechamp is brewing tea for you." I raised my voice to prevent her from immediately contradicting me. "Wait in the restaurant, on your left as you enter. Miss Millechamp is brewing tea for you."
[76] "So that's Miss Pemakh, is it? Can she see?"
[77] "Yes, she is. This has certainly shocked her, but she has been very rational about it. Come on, I'll take you in. Having a cup of tea while waiting for the police will make you feel better."
[78] I put my arm around her shoulder and led her down the path. After settling her comfortably at the table, I rushed to the phone booth.
[79] 2
[80] A cold voice said, "Croedin Police Station."
[81] "Is Inspector Hatchet there?"
[82] The voice suddenly became cautious:
[83] "I don't know. Who is this?"
[84] "Tell him it's Colin Loom."
[85] "Please wait."
[86] I waited. Then Dick Hakast's voice came over the line.
[87] "Is that Colin? It's been a while. Where are you?"
[88] "Crofton. To be precise, I'm on the floor of 19 Wilbraham Crescent. There's a man lying there, dead, I think stabbed. Probably died about half an hour ago."
[89] "Who found him? You?"
[90] "No, a stranger. A girl came running out of the house, almost knocking me over. She said there was a man lying on the floor of the house, dead. A blind woman almost stepped on his body."
[91] "You're not pulling my leg, are you?" Dick asked skeptically.
[92] "I admit, it sounds incredible, but that's the truth. The woman is the owner of the house, Miss Mirella Pembleton."
[93] "The one who almost tripped over the dead man?"
[94] "Not like you think. If she was blind, she wouldn't have noticed the dead man lying there."
[95] "I'll be right there. Wait for me there. How did you take care of the girl?"
[96] "Miss Pemah is brewing tea for her."
[97] Dic commented that the arrangement sounded somewhat soothing.
[98] Chapter Two
[99] At 19 Wilbraham Crescent, the police officers had arrived. A forensic expert, a photographer, and a fingerprint examiner were present. They worked in an orderly manner, with each person performing their designated task efficiently.
[100] The last to arrive was Inspector Hakast, a tall man with expressive eyebrows and a stern expression. He observed that all the work he had arranged was proceeding smoothly. He glanced at the corpse, exchanged a few brief words with the forensic expert, and then went to the dining room. There, he found three people seated with three empty teacups in front of them. They were Miss Pemah, Colin Lum, and a tall girl with brown curls. The girl's eyes were wide with fear. "Very nice," the inspector remarked in his usual witty manner.
[101] He introduced himself to Miss Pema.
[102] "Detective Inspector Dick Hakast."
[103] He knew something about Miss Pema, despite their lines of work never intersecting. He had seen her a few times before, knowing her to be a teacher at the Allenburg Institute, teaching blind script to disabled children. The discovery of a man dead of murder in such a clean, simple house seemed improbable. But often the most improbable things are the most common.
[104] "This is a truly awful thing, Miss Pema," he said, "and I'm afraid it's quite a shock to you. I need to get a clear understanding of the whole incident from you. I know -" he glanced quickly at the police report he had been given, "Hilary Webb was the one who actually found the body. Miss Pema, if you allow me to use your kitchen, I would like to bring Miss Webb there and speak with her privately."
[105] He opened the door connecting the dining room and the kitchen, waiting for the girl to enter. A young plainclothes detective was already in the kitchen, sitting at a table with a Formica-topped surface, writing something quietly.
[106] "This chair looks quite comfortable," Hakcastle said, pulling a modern-style Windsor chair.
[107] Hilary Webber sat nervously, her big fearful eyes staring straight at him.
[108] Hakcastle almost said, "Dear, I won't eat you," but he held back and said instead,
[109] "Don't worry. We just want to know what happened. Your name is Hilary Webber. Your address?"
[110] "14 Palmerston Road, a little further down the gas works."
[111] "Okay, next. I assume you have a job?"
[112] "Yes, I'm a stenographer typist, and I work at Miss Martin's Document Printing Agency."
[113] "Cavendish Document Printing Agency, is that the full name?"
[114] "Yes."
[115] "How long have you been working there?"
[116] "About a year. Well, to be exact, ten months."
[117] "Okay. Now tell me, how did you end up at 19 Wilbraham Crescent today?"
[118] "Well, it's like this. Miss Pember called the typewriting agency and asked for a stenographer to come here at 3 pm. So when I came back from lunch, Miss Martin sent me here."
[119] "Is that just a regular shift, or do you guys arrange these kinds of jobs differently?"
[120] "Actually, it's not exactly like that. Miss Pember specifically asked for me to come."
[121] "Ms. Pemakh specifically asked for you to come." Mr. Hakast's eyebrows remained unmoving. "I see, because you worked for her before?"
[122] "But I didn't." Sheila immediately answered.
[123] "You didn't work for her before? Are you sure?"
[124] "Yes, I'm positive. I mean, she's not the kind of person you forget. That's what's strange about it."
[125] "It is quite unusual. Well, let's not discuss that for now. When did you get here?"
[126] "It must have been around three o'clock, because that cuckoo clock—" She immediately stopped. Her eyes widened. "How strange. It's so strange. I didn't really pay attention to the time then."
[127] "Did you notice anything, Miss Webber?"
[128] "How could I have not noticed those clocks?"
[129] "What about those clocks?"
[130] "The cuckoo clock struck three, but the others were almost an hour ahead. How strange!"
[131] "That is strange," the detective replied. "So, when was the first time you found the body?"
[132] "It wasn't until I turned around the sofa that I noticed it. There he was, lying there. It was terrible, so terrible…"
[133] "Terrible! I agree. Do you know the man? Have you seen him before?"
[134] "No, I haven't."
[135] "Are you sure you've never seen him? He might look different now than when you last saw him. Think carefully. Are you absolutely certain you've never seen him before?"
[136] "Absolutely."
[137] "Alright. That's enough about that. So, what did you do next?"
[138] "What did I do?"
[139] "Yes."
[140] "Why are you asking? I didn't do anything, absolutely nothing. I couldn't have done anything."
[141] "I understand. You didn't touch him at all?"
[142] "Oh, yes, I did. I touched him to see if... I mean, just to confirm, but he was so cold, and then, then my hand got covered in blood. It was so horrible, sticky."
[143] She started shaking.
[144] "Okay, okay," Detective Hakast said in a soothing tone, "Let's move on from that. Forget about the blood. What happened next?"
[145] "I don't know... Yes, she came back then."
[146] "You mean Miss Pemakho?"
[147] "Yes. I didn't realize it was Miss Pemakho. She just happened to come in with a shopping bag."
[148] "So, what did you say?"
[149] "I think I didn't say anything... I tried to speak, but I couldn't make a sound. It felt like my throat was being squeezed."
[150] The detective nodded.
[151] "Then, she said, 'Who's there?' and she came around the sofa, and I thought, I thought she was going to step on him. That's when I screamed... Once I started screaming, I couldn't stop. I don't know how I just ran out of the house and out the front door."
[152] "Like a ghost," the detective remembered Colin's description.
[153] Shira Webber looked at him with eyes full of pain and fear, and unexpectedly said,
[154] "I'm sorry."
[155] "There's nothing to be sorry about. You did well. Don't think about it anymore. Oh, and one more thing, why were you in that room?"
[156] "Why?" She looked confused.
[157] "Yes. You may have arrived a few minutes early, I think, and then you rang the doorbell. But if no one answered, how did you get in?"
[158] "Oh, that. She told me to come in."
[159] "Who told you?"
[160] "Miss Pemaroo."
[161] "But I thought you hadn't spoken to her."
[162] "Yes, we hadn't. Miss Martindale told me to wait in the sitting room on the right in the hall."
[163] Hakast pondered, "So that's how it is!"
[164] Sheila Weber timidly asked:
[165] "And is there anything else?"
[166] "I think so. I'd like you to stay here for about ten minutes, in case I think of anything else to ask you. Then, I'll send a police car to take you home. What's your family situation?"
[167] "My parents are dead. I live with my aunt."
[168] "What's her name?"
[169] "Mrs. Lott."
[170] The detective rose and held out his hand.
[171] "Thank you very much, Miss Webber," he said. "Have a good night's sleep and rest well. You need plenty of sleep after all this."
[172] She timidly smiled at him and then entered the dining room.
[173] "Take care of Miss Webber, Colin," the detective said. "Now, Miss Permshaw. Could you come here, please?"
[174] Hakast stretched out his hand to guide Miss Permshaw, but she firmly came over herself, feeling her way with her fingertips, and found a chair close to the wall, pulling it out a foot's distance and sitting down.
[175] Hakast closed the door. Just as he was about to speak, Miss Millicent Permshaw suddenly asked, "Who is the young man?"
[176] "His name is Colin Lamb."
[177] "He has already told me that. But who is he? How did he get here?"
[178] Hakaste looked somewhat surprised at her.
[179] "When Miss Weaver screamed and ran out of the house saying there was a murder, he happened to be passing by the street. After confirming what happened inside the house, he called us and we let him wait back."
[180] "You call him Colin."
[181] "You are very observant, Miss Pemahox (the word 'meticulous' is not quite appropriate, but seems to be the most suitable one). Colin Lamm is my friend, but we haven't seen each other for a long time. He is an ocean biologist."
[182] "Oh! So that's it."
[183] "Now, Miss Pemahox, if you could tell me about this strange incident, I would be very happy."
[184] "I would be glad to. But there is nothing much to say."
[185] "I suppose you have been living here for some time, haven't you?"
[186] "I have been living here since 1950. I am... my profession is a teacher. When I was told that my deteriorating vision was incurable and that I would soon become blind, I studied Braille and other skills that could help the blind, hoping to become an expert in this field. I now have a job at the Allenberg Institute for Disabled Children."
[187] "Thank you. Now, tell me about what happened this afternoon. Are you waiting for a guest?"
[188] "No."
[189] "I will describe the physical features of the deceased to see if you can recall any specific person. His height is between 5 feet 9 inches and 10 inches, around sixty years old, with gray hair and brown eyes, clean-shaven beard, a thin face, and a strong chin. He is in good physical condition but not overweight. He was wearing a dark gray suit and well-groomed hands. He could be a banker, accountant, lawyer, or a professional in some industry. These descriptions remind you of anyone you know?"
[190] Miss Pemarcho carefully thought about the description before answering.
[191] "I cannot pinpoint it exactly because these are very common descriptions, and many people have these features. Perhaps I have seen or met someone like that in some occasion, but I cannot confirm who it is."
[192] "Have you received any letters recently from anyone planning to visit you?"
[193] "Absolutely not."
[194] "Good. Then, you called the Cavendish Agency to find a typist -"
[195] She interrupted him.
[196] "I'm sorry. I didn't do that."
[197] "You didn't call the Cavendish Typing Agency and ask for –" Hakast's eyes widened.
[198] "I don't have a phone at home."
[199] "There's a phone booth at the end of the street," Detective Hakast pointed out.
[200] "Yes, there is. But I assure you, Detective Hakast, I don't need a typist, and I haven't – I repeat, I haven't called the Cavendish Typing Agency to make any such request."
[201] "Did you specifically ask for Miss Sheila Weber?"
[202] "I've never heard of that name."
[203] Detective Hakast stared at her, feeling quite surprised.
[204] "You didn't lock the front door when you left," he pointed out.
[205] "I do that often during the day."
[206] "Maybe someone could have walked in."
[207] "It seems someone did during this incident," Miss Pemukho said coldly.
[208] "Miss Pemukho, according to the evidence provided by the forensic expert, the man died between 1:30 and 2:45. Where were you during that time?"
[209] Miss Pemukho thought for a moment.
[210] "By 1:30, I was either out or getting ready to go out. I had to go buy some things."
[211] "Can you tell me exactly where you went?"
[212] "Let me think. I went to the post office, a post office on Albion Road, to mail a package and buy some stamps; then I went to buy some everyday items, such as buttons and safety pins, at 'Field and Lane' fabric store; and then I came back. I can tell you the exact time I got home. When I got to the front gate, my cuckoo clock chimed three times 'cuckoo,' a sound that could be heard from the street."
[213] "What about your other clocks?"
[214] "What did you say?"
[215] "Your other clocks seem to be fast by more than an hour."
[216] "Fast? Do you mean the grandfather clock in the corner?"
[217] "Not just that one, all the clocks in the living room are fast."
[218] "I don't know what you mean by 'other clocks'. There are no other clocks in this living room."
[219] "Chapter 3"
[220] Detective Hakast was flabbergasted.
[221] "Ah, so, Miss Pemshaw. What about the Dresden porcelain clock on the mantelpiece? And the exquisite French clock, gilded, and the silver travel clock, and, oh yes, the clock with 'Rosemary' written on the face."
[222] This time, it was Miss Pemshaw's turn to be stunned.
[223] "Either you're going mad, or I am, Detective. I'm sure I don't have a Dresden porcelain clock, nor a French gilded clock, nor...what else did you say? Oh, right, the silver travel clock."
[224] "The silver travel clock," Detective Hakast mumbled.
[225] "I don't have that clock either. If you don't believe me, you can ask the woman who cleans my room. Her name is Mrs. Cotting."
[226] Inspector Hakast was taken aback. Miss Pemarcho seemed very certain, her tone sharp and decisive, convincing. He took a moment to ponder the situation. Then he stood up.
[227] "I'd like to know, Miss Pemarcho, if you mind coming with me to the next room to see these clocks?"
[228] "Of course not. Frankly, I'd like to see those clocks myself."
[229] "See?" Hakast felt confused.
[230] "Perhaps 'perceive' would be more accurate," Miss Pemarcho said. "But, Inspector, even a blind person, when they speak in ordinary terms, doesn't necessarily mean the ordinary meaning. When I say I want to 'see' those clocks, my actual intention is to 'perceive' them with my own fingers."
[231] Detective Hakast walked out of the kitchen, with Miss Pemshaw following behind him, through the small hallway, and into the living room. The fingerprint technician looked up at him.
[232] "I've almost finished all the work, officer," he said. "You can touch anything you like."
[233] Detective Hakast nodded, picked up the small travel clock with the label "Rosemary" written on it, and placed it in Miss Pemshaw's hand. She carefully touched it.
[234] "This seems to be an ordinary travel clock," she said. "The kind with leather covering. It's not mine, Detective Hakast. I'm quite certain it wasn't in this room when I left at half past one."
[235] "Thank you."
[236] The inspector took the clock back from her hand. He carefully picked up the Dresden small porcelain clock from the mantelpiece.
[237] "Be careful," he said as he placed it in her hand, "it's fragile."
[238] Miss Pemaroo delicately touched the porcelain small clock with her delicate fingers. She shook her head. "This must be a charming little clock," she said, "but it's not mine. Where was it placed?"
[239] "On the right side of the mantelpiece."
[240] "It should be one of the candlesticks there," Miss Pemaroo said.
[241] "Yes," said Hakast, "there is one there, but it has been pushed to the edge."
[242] "You mean there's another clock?"
[243] "There are two more."
[244] Hakast took back the Dresden porcelain clock and handed her the French gilded clock. She quickly touched it and then returned it to him.
[245] "No, this one isn't mine either."
[246] He handed her the silver clock, and she gave it back to him in the same way.
[247] "There is usually only the grandfather clock in the room, placed in the corner next to the window—"
[248] "Yes."
[249] "And there is a cuckoo clock on the wall near the door."
[250] Hakaste found himself at a loss for words after that. He observed the woman in front of him, knowing she would not respond to his scrutiny, and felt a sense of relief. Her forehead was slightly furrowed in confusion. She suddenly spoke:
[251] "I don't understand what's going on. I really can't make sense of it."
[252] She extended her hand, knowing exactly where she was in the room, and quickly found a chair to sit down. Hakaste noticed the fingerprint technician standing by the door.
[253] "Did you check all the clocks?" he asked.
[254] "I checked everything, sir. The gilded clock has no fingerprints, which is normal since the surface of that material doesn't leave prints. The same goes for the porcelain clock. But there are no fingerprints on the leather travel clock or the silver clock, which is quite unusual. Moreover, all the clocks are not wound up, and they all stopped at the same time, 4:13 PM."
[255] "What about the other rooms?"
[256] "There were three to four different types of fingerprints found in the room, and it's likely that they all belong to women. All the items found in the deceased's pockets were placed on the table."
[257] Pointing in the direction of the person's head, he saw a small pile of items placed on the table. Hakaste walked over to take a closer look. There was a small wallet containing seven pounds, ten shillings, and some change, an unmarked silk handkerchief, a small box of digestive pills, and a business card. Hakaste bent down to look at it.
[258] R. H. Kouri, Esq.
[259] Great City Small Town Insurance Company
[260] 7 Danver Street,
[261] London W2.
[262] Hakakst returned to the sofa where Miss Pemuko was sitting.
[263] "Do you ever make appointments to see someone from the insurance company?"
[264] "Insurance company? No, absolutely not."
[265] "What about 'Metropolitan District Insurance Company'?" Hakakst said.
[266] Miss Pemaroo shook her head. "I've never heard of that company."
[267] "Have you ever considered getting any kind of insurance?"
[268] "No. I have fire and theft insurance with 'Jupiter Insurance Company', which has a branch here, and I don't have life insurance. I have no family or close relatives, so there's no need to insure my life."
[269] "I see," Hakaste said. "So, does the name Kirby have any connection to you? Mr. R. H. Kirby?"
[270] "Kirby?" she repeated the name and shook her head. "That's not a common name, is it? No, I don't think I've ever heard that name or known anyone by that name. Is that the name of the deceased?"
[271] "Maybe," said Hakaste.
[272] Miss Pemmerhoven hesitated for a moment. Then she said:
[273] "Should I go, touch—"
[274] He quickly understood her meaning.
[275] "You mean to 'feel' it yourself, Miss Pemmerhoven? Is that too much to ask of you? I'm not very good at doing such things, but compared to a verbal description, your fingers might give you a better idea of what the person looked like."
[276] "Yes, that's what I mean," said Miss Pemuk. "I admit that doing this won't be pleasant, but if you think it will be helpful, I'm willing to do it."
[277] "Thank you," said Hakast. "I'll take you there."
[278] He led her around the sofa, indicating for her to kneel down and then gently guiding her hand to the dead man's face. She was very calm and emotionless. Her fingers ran over the dead man's hair and eyes, lingering for a moment at the left ear before moving on to the bridge of the nose, mouth, and chin. Then she shook her head and stood up.
[279] "I have a clear image of his appearance now," she said. "But I'm sure I've never seen him before, I don't recognize him."
[280] The fingerprint examiner packed up his toolbox, left the room, and poked his head back in.
[281] "They're going to move him," he said, indicating the corpse. "Can he be moved?"
[282] "Move him," Detective Hakaste said. "Come and sit over here, Miss Pemukho."
[283] He arranged her to sit in a chair in the corner. Two men entered the room. Soon, Mr. Kuri's body was carried out. Detective Hakaste went outside to the front door and then returned to the living room. He sat next to Miss Pemukho.
[284] "This is quite a strange case, Miss Pemukho," he said. "I'd like to go over the key points of the incident again to make sure I have it right. If I've said anything wrong, please correct me. You didn't have any appointments for any visitors today, you didn't consult or intend to take out any kind of insurance, and you didn't receive any letters saying that an insurance company's representative would be visiting you today, right?"
[285] "Absolutely correct."
[286] "You did not need a stenographer's service, and you did not call the Calverdish Document Service and request someone to come here at three o'clock."

Therefore, it may have been deliberately arranged to have central heating instead of a fireplace during the mistress's gathering, so that the crime could be committed without being noticed once the lights were turned off.  There are two doors leading to the living room where the crime scene is located. Another door with oiled hinges and just recently opened. There was a table blocking the second door, but it was later moved to the wall.  The table that was placed against the second door was recently moved. It might be intentional on the part of the hostess, as it is her own house.  The next day after the incident, the police found the wilted violet in the vase to be the only suspicious clue in the room.  Before the incident, Miss Blacklock was seated at the table, holding the vase of purple lilies in her hands. Ceramic lamps on the table. Based on the clues, the mistress Blacklock extinguishes the table lamp with water from the vase in her hand when Rudi enters, then exits through another door lubricated with oil, making little noise when opening it, and circles around to Rudi's back to shoot and kill him with a gun.

Letizia's letter to her sister Charlotte mentions that Charlotte is undergoing iodine therapy.  Letizia's sister has some deformities in her appearance. The hostess wore a short necklace made of large faux pearls around her neck, which appeared somewhat out of place with her clothing. When the mistress's pearl necklace fell, she covered her throat with her hand and rushed out of the living room. The mistress's pearl necklace is a fake. Therefore, the hostess Letitia Blacklock may be impersonated by her sister Charlotte, who may have a goiter treated with iodine, and could only cover her neck scar from the surgery with an abrupt and incongruous pearl necklace, and had to cover her throat when the pearl fell off.  Dora Bunner calls the hostess Lotte, which is Charlotte Blacklock.  The hostess reminded Bonner, "Don't do that, Bonner. You know I've asked you —" Bonner Miss said she forgot. Rudi met the mistress before he died, Rudi and the mistress, along with her sister, had lived together, and Rudi recognized the mistress. Based on the clues, the mistress Leticia Blacklock is actually her sister Charlotte disguised, so Dora Bunner calls her Lois and is silenced when she tries to reveal her true identity, Rudy is killed after recognizing her real identity, and uses an abrupt and incongruous pearl necklace to cover the surgical scar on her neck.

When asking Dora Bunner, no reason needs to be given. No matter what she is asked, Miss Bunner, who loves to talk, is always ready to provide an answer. Dora Bunner called the mistress Lotte, which was Charlotte Blacklock. The hostess reminded Bonner, "Don't do that, Bonner. You know I've called you——" Bonner Miss said she forgot.  Dora was very angry when she mistakenly called the mistress Lois again. Miss Blacklock exclaimed, "Dora, forgive me. I had no choice. I had to —" when she heard Dora's voice.  Miss Blacklock, the hostess, was preparing the birthday cake, saying that it was worth dying for such a cake. The woman tells Bonnet to go to her bedside to find aspirin when she is going to sleep but can't find it. Based on the clues provided, Dora is always chatty and forgetful, repeatedly referring to the female owner as Lotty. The female owner is concerned about her true identity being exposed, so when Bonner goes to sleep and cannot find aspirin, she switches the aspirin on her bedside table with poison, killing Dora.

Letitia Blacklock had served as a secretary for the millionaire Randall and had a close relationship with him. Letitia Blacklock will inherit her wealth upon the death of the wealthy man. Charlotte had been deformed, so she never saw anyone and stayed indoors.  Dora says that Charlotte bravely endures the painful torment, and her courage and endurance deserve praise, no matter what good rewards she receives, she truly deserves them. Mr. Blacklock's father was conservative and could not tolerate any new ideas or methods. Based on the above clues, Charlotte pretended to be her sister Letitia Blacklock in order to obtain the inheritance of the wealthy Randall. She had previously been deformed and suffered greatly, and her own father did not seek new methods to treat her. She hoped to obtain this inheritance to start a new life and believed she deserved a good reward.

Phila is a young woman with few words, but good manners. Miss Marple said that the village nowadays is full of outsiders who have no local ties, and they just settle down there. Phil is just a temporary gardener. So, it is possible that Philippa is not just a local, but an outsider, and her identity is related to the mistress, which is why the mistress kept her around.  When Randall, the wealthy man, designated his heirs, he begrudgingly wrote down his niece, Sonya's daughter, as the second heir in case the wife passed away before him.  When the mistress found out that the police suspected the niece of the wealthy man, she was extremely agitated. Therefore, the hostess should not want the suspicion to fall on her niece.  The hostess is a kind-hearted and compassionate person. The mistress had lived with Sonya. The hostess recognizes Sonya but for some reason immediately changes her tone.  All of Sonya's photos were taken from the album. Based on the above clues, the hostess is concerned that the police may discover her niece's identity from Sonia's photo, as she can recognize her niece from Sonia's face, which is actually Felicity. Out of her innate kindness, in her subconscious, she intends to help alleviate any possible anxiety she may have had. She thinks that once she inherits the money, she will treat Felicity well.

The discovery of the withered violet in the vase the day after the incident was the only suspicious clue in the room. The water in the violet hyacinth vase is gone. There are burn marks on the table. All the lights went out at the time of the incident. Dora said she heard a creak when the light went out. Miss Marple spilled some water from the vase, which fell on the frayed wire, causing the fuse to blow, and all the lights should be out. Miss Marple pressed the switch, and a spark flew from the place where the cat had bitten and the water had soaked. Based on the above clues, the killer caused a short circuit in the table lamp by pouring water from the vase onto the exposed wires, which resulted in burn marks on the table and all the lights being extinguished. Miss Marple accidentally recreated the scene, which is why the lamp on the table was replaced the next day to prevent the discovery of evidence of the crime. The killer used the short circuit to create darkness during the crime, and the lamp had already been damaged by the fire.

[3] Extracted from Yu Chuan's "Chien Yeh Collection"
[4] Chapter 1: Theater Audience and Corpses
[5] The opening of the 1920s drama festival was embarrassing. Eugene O'Neill forgot to create a new play in time, so he couldn't get financial support from the "cultured" people. As for the "common people", after watching a few passionless plays, they gave up the formal theater and went to the movie house to find simpler pleasure.
[6] On Monday evening, September 24th, a light drizzle covered the brightly lit Broadway theater district from 37th Street to Columbus Circle. Desolate theater managers and directors could be seen everywhere. Several plays were canceled on the spot by higher-ups, hoping that God and the weather bureau would witness their plight. The rain kept people who should have been at the theater at home by their radios and card tables. Only a few brave souls ventured out into the deserted streets in the rain. Broadway was indeed in a gloomy mood.
[7] However, on the sidewalk in front of the Roman Theater on 47th Street, west of "White Street", there was a crowd of spectators who only came out during the mid-period of the theater festival when the weather was fine. The signboard of "The Gunfight" shone brilliantly under the decorative awning of the theater entrance. The cashier skillfully served the crowd of people waiting in front of the "Today's Performance" window. The doorman wore a sober uniform of yellow and blue, his demeanor refined by the passage of time, and was therefore very conspicuous. He bowed to lead the evening's audience into the front row of the auditorium. These spectators wore high hats and leather coats, with satisfied expressions on their faces, as if nothing could stop them from watching "The Gunfight" performance.
[8] In the latest theater on Broadway, people were hurriedly looking for their seats, obviously a little anxious, as the play's noisy characteristics were well known. At this point, the last chattering audience stopped, the last audience to arrive was tripped by his neighbor, and the lights gradually dimmed, and the curtain slowly rose. A gunshot echoed, a man screamed... the show began.
[9] "The Gunfight" is the first play of the drama festival to use the characteristic sound effects of the mob. Automatic pistols, machine guns, attacks on nightclubs, mob killings that kill enemies with loud noises - all the clichéd ways of romanticizing the mob society were woven into the fast-paced three-act play. It exaggeratedly reflected the era - a little vulgar, a little lowbrow, but all in all, it satisfied the audience who watched the play. Therefore, whether it was sunny or rainy, the play was always full and sold out. The situation in the theater tonight was enough to prove its popularity.
[10] The performance progressed smoothly. The first act reached its climax with an explosion, and the audience shuddered. The rain had stopped, and people used the ten-minute break after the first act to step out of the theater and breathe in the fresh air after the rain. Then, the curtain slowly rose, and the second act began. The explosions on the stage were even louder. With the sharp-tongued dialogue behind the stage lights, the second act quickly entered the crucial moment. The slight commotion at the back of the theater did not attract attention, as it was normal in the noise and darkness. It seemed that no one noticed anything was wrong, and the plot continued to unfold with a bang. However, the noise of the disturbance gradually increased. At this point, several audience members in the back row on the left began to stir in their seats, angrily defending their rights. This protest was highly contagious, and soon dozens of eyes turned to the front row of the auditorium.
[11] Suddenly, a piercing scream echoed through the theater. The audience, engrossed in the rapid events unfolding on stage, craned their necks expectantly in the direction of the scream, hoping for a new dramatic twist in the plot.
[12] The theater lights suddenly snapped on, illuminating bewildered, terrified, and enraptured faces, all satisfied with the plot. Near the leftmost closed exit, a tall policeman stood, grabbing the arm of a slightly tense-looking man. The policeman pushed away a crowd of inquisitive people with a loud voice, shouting, "Stay in your seats and don't move!"
[13] The audience burst into laughter.
[14] But the smiles quickly faded. As the audience began to realize that even the actors looked confused and hesitant, despite continuing to recite their lines behind the stage lights, occasionally casting puzzled glances at the front row of the auditorium. People stood up from their seats, uneasy in the face of the anticipated tragedy. The officer's authoritative voice continued to roar, "I said, sit still! Stay where you are!"
[15] The audience suddenly realized that this was not a play but reality. Women screamed, desperately clutching their companions. The upper-level audience was in a panic, despite not being able to see what was happening downstairs.
[16] The officer turned sharply to a small, dark-skinned man dressed in evening attire, standing nearby and fidgeting with his hands.
[17] "Mr. Pensler, I need you to close every exit immediately and make sure they are all locked," he barked. "Assign a usher to each entrance to prevent anyone from entering or leaving. Have someone guard the alley until the police arrive. Move quickly, Mr. Pensler, or there will be trouble."
[18] Some excited audience members disregarded the officer's loud warnings and crowded around to ask questions. The small, dark-skinned man pushed them away and hurried off.
[19] The officer spread his legs and stood at the last exit on the left, using his massive frame to block a person lying on the floor between two rows of seats. The person was dressed in evening attire and lay in an odd position. The officer looked up, grabbed the trembling man beside him, and quickly scanned the back of the auditorium.
[20] "Hey, Nelson!" he called.
[21] A tall, blond-haired man quickly emerged from the small room next to the main exit, pushing through the crowd and approaching the policeman. He looked sharply at the motionless body on the floor.
[22] "What happened, Dohr?" he asked.
[23] "You'd better ask this guy," the policeman said sternly, shaking the arm he was holding. "Someone died, and this one—" he glared fiercely at the huddled little man, "Bosack, William Bosack. Mr. Bosack here says,” Dohr stammered, "Mr. Bosack says he heard the dead man whisper that he was murdered."
[24] Nelson stared at the body, dumbfounded.
[25] The policeman bit his lip. "This is a real pain in the ass, Harry," he croaked. "I'm the only cop here, and I have to deal with a bunch of hysterical idiots... I need your help."
[26] "Sure, whatever you say—this is quite a mystery."
[27] Doris suddenly turned around and shouted at the man sitting three rows ahead who was staring at him, "Hey, get down here! And you guys, back to your seats! Now! Anyone who meddles gets a punch from me!"
[28] He turned to Nelson. "Harry, get back to your office and call headquarters. Tell them there's a murder here. Have them send a squad over—bring a lot of them. Tell them it's at the theater—they'll know what to do. And, Harry—take my whistle and blow it outside. I need help."
[29] Nelson walked back through the crowd, and Doris called after him, "Harry, make sure they send old Quin over."
[30] The man with light brown hair disappeared from view, returning to his office. Soon, a sharp whistle echoed through the sidewalk in front of the theater.
[31] The dark-skinned theater manager followed Doral's orders to have people guard the exits and alleys, and then he rushed back through the crowd. His evening dress shirt was wrinkled, and he wiped his forehead, looking flustered. As he turned to go forward, a woman stopped him.
[32] She said sternly, "Mr. Pensler, what gives this policeman the right to keep us here? I tell you, I have the right to leave! I don't care what's going on here - it's none of my business - it's your business - tell him not to do this stupid thing of locking up innocent people!"
[33] The little man tried to escape while stammering, "Oh, ma'am, please listen to me. I'm sure this officer knows what he's doing. Someone was killed here - it's serious. You don't see... I'm the theater manager, and I have to follow his orders... please calm down... be patient..."

Only an experienced actor could pull off a plan like this. After all, the process is simple; the hardest part is sticking to the schedule. If he was seen, he would have been disguised. The most dangerous part of his plan was – how to escape when he walked down the aisle, through the backstage entrance to the stage, while the ushers were there. He had observed the ushers while sitting next to Field. Of course, he knew that due to the nature of the performance, the ushers would be mostly faithful to their duties, and he counted on his disguise and syringe to help him through any unexpected situations. However, Maggie O'Connell did not do her job properly, so that was to his advantage. He proudly told me last night that he had prepared for emergencies... As for the backstage entrance, he knew from experience that everyone would be on stage and the technicians would be busy in their positions at that time... Remember, he planned the crime with the exact conditions in mind. If there were any dangers and uncertainties – well, isn't that the nature of an adventure? – he asked me with a smile last night; I had to admit that, if not for this, I would greatly admire his style."
[2190] The officer uneasily shifted the topic. "I hope I've made it clear how Barry committed the crime. As for our investigation... besides the reasoning about the hat and knowing the identity of the killer, we still know nothing about the exact details of the crime. If you remember the evidence we gathered on Thursday night, you will understand that there was nothing to go on. What we hope most is that there is some clue in the files we need to find that is related to Barry. Even then, it's not enough... so the next step, the officer sighed, "is to find the secret compartment on the canopy of the bed in Field's apartment. This work has been done by Ellery from beginning to end. We found that Field did not have a safe, no mailbox, no other residence, no intimate neighbors or business partners, and those files were not in his office. After elimination, Ellery insisted that these files were in Field's room. You know how the search ended - completely through Ellery's genius reasoning. We found Morgan's files, discovered the material needed by Croning about the mafia activities - by the way, Tim, I keenly noticed what happened when we started the big clean-up - we finally found a bundle of miscellaneous files, including Michaels and Barry's... Tim, you will remember, Ellery deduced from handwriting analysis that we might find Barry's original files - and indeed we did.
[2191] "Mickles' case was quite interesting. He was sent to Elmira on a 'minor theft' charge thanks to Field's clever manipulation of the law. However, Field possessed evidence of the true crime Mickles had committed and hid it in his favorite collection, intending to use it at a later date. This Field, what a cunning man... After Mickles was released, Field used these documents to coerce Mickles into doing various tasks for him without any remorse.
[2192] "For a long time, Michael has been searching for those files. His eagerness, you can imagine. He would go to the apartment whenever he had the chance. After one failure after another, he became desperate. I have no doubt that when Field found out that Michael was rummaging through his apartment day after day, he must have been laughing behind his back... On Monday night, Michael went home to sleep as he said. But on Tuesday morning, when he read the newspaper and learned that Field had been murdered, he realized it was all over. He had to search desperately for those files - if he couldn't find them, the police might find them, and then he would be finished. So, on Tuesday morning, he risked being caught by the police and returned to Field's house. Of course, the whole story about the check was just nonsense.
[2193] "But let's go back to Barry. We found a file labeled 'Miscellaneous' in the hat, detailing an unsavory matter. To abbreviate, Stephen Barry has black blood in his veins. Born into a poor family in the South, there is concrete evidence - letters, birth certificates, and so on - proving his black heritage. As we know, Field has made a business out of pursuing such things. He somehow acquired these documents, how long ago we do not know, but it must have been a long time. He had then discovered Barry's identity, finding him a struggling actor living in poverty and penniless. Field decided to leave him be for the time being. Once Barry made it big or became famous, there would be plenty of time to extort him. What Field did not anticipate was Barry's engagement to the daughter of a millionaire, the aristocratic socialite Frances Evans-Pope. It goes without saying that if Frances Evans-Pope were to find out about Barry's mixed heritage, the consequences would be dire. Furthermore, it is crucial to note that Barry had become impoverished due to gambling. His earnings had gone into the pockets of the racecourse bookmaker's agent, and he owed a significant amount of money, which he would never be able to repay with his current means, unless he married Frances. In fact, he was so destitute that he secretly urged her to marry him as soon as possible. I have always been curious about how sincerely he treated Frances. However, to be fair, I do not believe he married her solely for the money. I think he genuinely loved her - but who doesn't? But who doesn't?"
[2194] The old man smiled as he reminisced, continuing, "Not long ago, Field brought those documents to Barry – of course, secretly. Barry gave him all the money he could, but it was barely enough to satisfy the insatiable extortionist. With no other option, he could only keep delaying Field. But Field himself was in a bind due to gambling, trying to 'recoup' funds through one small deal after another. Barry was at a dead end, realizing that unless he made Field forever silent, he would lose everything. So he planned this murder. He understood that even if he somehow managed to gather the $50,000 Field demanded – clearly an impossible task – even if he got the original documents, Field would still ruin his hopes by spreading the word. The only way out was – eliminate Field. And he did."
[2195] "Black blood, huh?" Crooning grumbled, "Poor fellow."
[2196] "You couldn't tell from his looks," said Sampson, "he looked just as white as you and me."
[2197] "Barry is not like a pure black man," the officer countered, "He has one drop of black blood in his veins – just one drop, but that's enough for the Evans-Pope family... Continue on. After reading these documents, we understood everything: who did it, how it was done, and the motive. But we have to make a judgment on the evidence to convict. You can't accuse someone of murder without evidence... er, what do we have? Nothing!
[2198] "Let's discuss some useful clues that could serve as evidence. The handbag of the woman - eliminate. It's worthless, you know. The source of the poison - can't find it. By the way, Barry did it according to Dr. Jones' method - the toxicologist Jones. Barry bought regular gasoline, distilled it to get tetraethyl lead. No trace left. Another possible clue - Monte Field's hat, but it's gone... Six empty tickets - we've never seen them, and the chances of seeing them are slim. The only physical evidence - those documents - only explain the motive, but can't prove anything. With this evidence, any member of Morgan or Field's gang could have committed the crime."
[2199] "The only hope of securing incriminating evidence lies in sending someone to sneak into Barry's apartment at night, hoping to find the hat, tickets, or other clues, such as poison or poisonous instruments. I have engaged a specialist in burglary for this purpose, who will break into Barry's apartment on Friday night while he is at the theater performing, but no such clues have been found. The hat, tickets, and poison have all been destroyed. It is clear that Barry did it, we can be sure."
[2200] "I gathered a group of Monday night viewers in desperation and held a meeting in the hope that someone would remember seeing Barry that night. You know, sometimes people forget things due to tension or excitement, but then they remember later. But this time it didn't work either. The only valuable testimony was from the boy selling orange juice, who saw Field pick up a handbag used at the evening party in the alley. However, this had nothing to do with Barry. Remember, on Thursday night, when we questioned the cast members, we didn't get any direct evidence either.
[2201] "So we have a perfect, hypothetical statement of fact to present to the jury, with no concrete evidence. A clever defense lawyer could easily refute our case. It's mostly indirect evidence based on reasoning. You and I both know how much of a chance we have in court... Then, my real trouble came, and Ellery was leaving town.
[2202] "I racked my brain - I was left with little. How can I convict someone without evidence? It's so frustrating. Ellery sent me a telegram with a suggestion that helped me one last time."
[2203] "A suggestion?" asked Cronin.
[2204] "He suggested that I personally engage in extortion..."
[2205] "You personally extort?" Sampson looked at him. "I don't understand."
[2206] "Trust Ellery, he's good at solving puzzles." The police officer refutes, "I immediately understand that the only thing I can do is fabricate evidence!"
[2207] Sampson and Cronin frown in confusion.
[2208] "It's simple," Quine says, "Field was killed by an unusual poison. The reason Field was killed was because he blackmailed Barry. If Barry was blackmailed in the same situation, he would use poison again - probably the same poison. My hypothesis is reasonable, right? I don't need to say that you both know, 'once bitten, twice shy.' As for Barry, if I can lure him into using tetraethyl lead on someone else, I can catch him! This poison is almost unknown - but I don't need to explain further. You can see that if I catch him with tetraethyl lead on him, that's all the evidence I need.
[2209] "How to accomplish this feat is another matter... The situation was perfect for blackmailing. In fact, I have the original documents about Barry's background and impure blood. Barry thought these documents had been destroyed - he had no reason to suspect that the ones he got from Field were carefully forged. If I blackmail him, then his situation will be the same again. So he must resort to the same tactics.
[2210] "So I took advantage of our friend Charles Michaels. I used Michaels only because, in Barry's eyes, Michaels was Field's friend, henchman, and loyal partner, and it was reasonable for him to possess the original documents. I had Michaels write a letter, dictated by me. I had Michaels write it because Barry had dealt with Field and might recognize Michaels' handwriting. This seemed like a small problem, but I couldn't take any risks. If this plan went wrong, Barry would immediately recognize it, and I would never catch him."
[2211] "In the letter, I attached an original document to show that this new blackmail threat was potent. I claimed that Field had given Barry a copy - the attached document proved my point. Barry didn't doubt that Michaels was imitating his master and blackmailing him. The wording was like a final ultimatum. I set a time and place, and in short, the scheme worked...
[2212] "I think that's all, gentlemen. Barry came, with his faithful little syringe subcutaneously injected with tetraethyl lead, and a bottle of wine - you see, except for the location, it was exactly the same as the Field case. I instructed my man - Ritter - not to take a risk. As soon as he recognized Barry, he aimed his gun at him and sounded the alarm. Fortunately, we were almost right behind them in the bushes. Barry was desperate, and if he had had even the slightest chance, he would have killed Ritter and committed suicide."
[2213] The officer finished speaking and sighed, leaning forward to snort some snuff, and the room fell silent.
[2214] Sampson shifted in his chair. "It sounds like a thriller, Quin," he said admiringly, "but there are a few things I don't understand. For example, since tetraethyl lead is unknown to people, how did Barry discover it - to the point where he could refine it himself?"
[2215] "Oh," the officer smiled, "Ever since Jones described this poison, this has bothered me. Even after catching Barry, I was still in the dark. But this shows how stupid I am - the answer has been right in front of my nose. Do you remember, when we were at the Eves-Pope estate, a doctor named Cornish was introduced? This doctor is a private friend of the old financier, and both of them are interested in medicine. In fact, I remember Ellery asking, 'Did Eves-Pope recently donate $100,000 to the Chemical Research Foundation?' Indeed, it was. One evening a few months ago, a meeting was held at the Eves-Pope house, and Barry happened to hear about tetraethyl lead. Through Cornish's introduction, a group of scientists visited this financial giant to request funding for the foundation. The evening's conversation naturally turned to rumors in medicine and recent scientific discoveries. Barry admitted that he had overheard the council member, a famous toxicologist, introducing this poison to the members. At the time, Barry didn't think he would ever use this knowledge; when he decided to kill Field, he saw the superiority of this poison and its difficult traceability."
[2216] "What was the significance of the message you sent me through Louis Ponzel on Thursday night, Inspector?" Cromwell asked curiously, "Do you remember? You asked me to observe whether Ponzel and Ponzel knew each other when they met at Louin? As I reported to you, I asked Louin, and he denied knowing Ponzel. What's going on?"
[2217] "Ponzel," the policeman whispered, "Ponzel always piques my curiosity, Tim. When I sent him to you, remember, I hadn't made any deductions about the hat... I sent him to you out of curiosity. I thought that if Louin recognized him, it might suggest a connection between Ponzel and Field. My idea wasn't confirmed, and I didn't have high hopes to begin with. Ponzel might have known Field outside, while Louin didn't know. On the other hand, I didn't want Ponzel to hang around the theater that morning; it was beneficial for both of us for him to run errands."
[2218] "Oh, I hope you're satisfied with the package of newspapers I sent you according to your request," Cromwell smiled.
[2219] "What about the anonymous letter that Morgan received? Was it a cover-up or something else?" Sampson asked.
[2220] "It was a deceptive trick," Quayne said solemnly. "Barry explained it to me last night. He heard that Morgan threatened to kill Field. Of course, he didn't know that Field was blackmailing Morgan. But he thought that if he could trick Morgan into coming to the theater on Monday night, it would create a strong false lead. If Morgan didn't come, there would be no loss. That's how he operated: he chose ordinary cheap paper, put on gloves, and printed the letter at a print shop in a messy way, signed it with a meaningless initial, and then mailed it from the post office. He was careful with his fingerprints, so he couldn't be traced from the letter. Coincidentally, Morgan fell for it and came
[2221] Sampson nodded. "I have one more question. How did Barry arrange for the tickets? Was it all his doing?"
[2222] "Of course, it was. Barry convinced Field that, for fairness, the meeting and the document exchange should take place secretly in the theater. Field agreed and was easily convinced to buy eight tickets at the ticket office. He realized that, for secrecy, he needed to buy six additional tickets. He gave Barry seven and kept one for himself, which he destroyed immediately."
[2223] The officer stood up, smiling tiredly. "Juna! Add some coffee," he whispered.
[2224] Sampson waved Juna away. "Thank you, Quin, I have to go. Cromwell and I have a lot of things to deal with regarding this gang. But I can't leave until I hear the whole story from you... Quin, old friend, I truly mean it, you did an incredible job."
[2225] "I've never heard of such a thing," Cromwell said sincerely. "A puzzle to solve, and such a perfect reasoning from start to finish!"
[2226] "Really?" the officer asked calmly. "I'm glad, gentlemen. All the credit goes to Ellery. I'm so proud of my son..."
[2227] Sampson and Cronin left, and Juna went back to the kitchen to wash the breakfast dishes. The officer turned to the desk, picked up a pen, and quickly read the letter he had written to his son. He sighed and continued writing.
[2228] Forget what I just wrote. It's been over an hour since then. Sampson and Cronin came by, and I told them all about the work we did on the case. I've never seen such a pair! They were like children, listening to a fairy tale... As I said, I know how little I've done, and how much you've done. I'm looking forward to you finding a good girl to marry, and then the Quin family will settle down and live peacefully in Italy...
[2229] When are you coming home? Don't think I'm rushing you, but I'm so lonely, son. I... no, I mean, I'm selfish and tired. An old relic like me needs some care. You'll be home soon, won't you? Juna sends his greetings. That mischievous fellow is washing dishes in the kitchen, making my ears ring.
[2230] Love, Dad

keypoints: The deceased died during the second act performance. The deceased is Field. There was no hat at the scene of Field's death.  Jesse still had his hat on when he served soda to Fielding after the second act curtain went up.  So the murderer took away Field's hat. So the hat may contain important documents that are difficult to remove. The remains of Field contain books about handwriting. Field had practiced different styles of handwriting. Field possesses Morgan's extortion documents and proposes to use these as evidence. Feldt repeatedly blackmailed Morgan. In Field's house, multiple hats were found with documents belonging to others.  Therefore, Field possessed important documents of others' scandals, and imitating handwriting may have been done for multiple times of blackmailing by making copies.  Field wrote the numbers 50,000 and 930 on the flyer. Field was still alive at 9:25. According to the clues, after Field's death, his hat was taken away, he had practiced different styles of handwriting, blackmailed Morgan multiple times, and his home had many hats embedded with important documents of others. The murderer had a transaction involving $50,000 with Field at 9:30, which was a blackmail scheme using the forged documents hidden in Field's hat. The murderer was dissatisfied with Field's blackmail and killed him.

During the second act, all exits were guarded by people. The hostess said there was nothing unusual in the aisle all night.  Therefore, the killer did not leave early. A search of the audience did not reveal any suspicious hats. While searching the theater, no extra hats were found. All the costumes for the actors in "Gunfight" are sourced from the same supplier M.  Therefore, the killer may have worn the uniform hat of the actor when entering the scene, and left with Field's hat on. Based on the clues provided, the killer did not leave the scene early, entered wearing a uniform hat, and left the scene wearing Field's hat after the police allowed the audience to leave.

Morgan rarely goes to the theater, but since he received complimentary tickets from the manager of the Roman Theater, he decided to attend tonight's performance. The theatre manager states that they do not have the paper to write an invitation letter to Morgan. He believes Nelson did it for promotion purposes. Nelson says that this idea doesn't apply to him at all. So, this letter doesn't seem to be written by the manager or any other staff member, but it could have been forged by Morgan or possibly by the killer to frame Morgan. Morgan had threatened to kill Field after breaking up with him as a partner. The evidence of Morgan's scandal in the field has been documented, and Morgan has been blackmailed. Four days before the incident, Mrs. Rathbone heard Morgan threatening to kill Field. Therefore, if the killer allows Morgan to be present, Morgan can become a major suspect. At the bottom of one of the hats hidden in Field's house, there is a name of Morgan. The hat of Field contained a file with Morgan's name. So these documents may be the blackmailing documents used by Field to blackmail Morgan. There was no hat at the scene of Field's death. Morgan explains that if he receives another extortion threat, he will turn himself in and expose Field. Therefore, Morgan is not the murderer, otherwise Morgan would have taken the hat, the hat with Morgan's name on the bottom would not be in Field's house.  According to the clues provided, Morgan has expressed that if he is threatened again, he will turn himself in and expose Field, and it is impossible for Morgan to kill Field without leaving a hat related to Morgan at Field's house, so the killer must have invited Morgan to the scene through a fake invitation letter in order to divert suspicion to Morgan.

The death scene of Field did not have his hat. A search of the audience did not reveal any suspicious hats. Therefore, the murderer took Field's hat, and the murderer was not an audience member.
